title: Back Porch
abstract: Back Porch Marcie Cohen Ferris, editor This extraordinary Snapshot: Climate issue marks the beginning of a year and more of contemplation—and celebration—of the thirtieth anniversary of the founding of Southern Cultures and the Center for the Study of the American South in 1993. The issue's focus on the climate crisis and how southern places and communities are experiencing and reacting to the daily impacts of climate change speaks also to the fifty-plus-year founding of the modern environmental movement in the United States and the first Earth Day, April 22, 1970. I was thirteen years old that spring and remember the student demonstrations, teach-ins, and images of smog-shrouded cities and sewage-filled rivers. In the Arkansas Delta, we were exposed to dangerous pesticides and defoliants used in industrial-scale cotton farming. The long and evolving history of environmentalism, combined with growing political activism, protest, and legislation, resulted in the creation of the US Environmental Protection Agency in December 1970 and the critical environmental regulatory actions that followed. Hundreds of laws and agencies have been attacked, rolled back, and revoked by the Trump administration and now the Republican majority in the House of Representatives.1 The collected powerful images of Snapshot: Climate are like a prescient family album of the region, caught at a specific moment in time and crisis as we stand at what the Washington Post called the "brink of catastrophic warming." As this issue was going to press, the UN Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's latest report indicated that without immediate, rapid response to phase out oil, gas, and coal, future generations will be unable to adapt to the changed environment. Higher temperatures will impede the growth of food crops and the survival of animals and their ecosystems. Heat waves, drought, famine, infectious disease, sea level rise, and more extreme weather disasters are our present and future.2 The photographers and writers in this issue testify to this experience. Through their eyes and voices, they bear witness to environmental losses, extractive industries, toxic chemical exposure, decline in animal populations, and climate-related ruin of both personal and public landmarks. They also testify to human resilience, joy, and beauty despite environmental trauma, anger, and injury—see Jenny Adler's haunting photograph of Florida's magnificent yet starving manatees. Or look at Monica Patrice Barra's beautiful photograph from Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana, where Hurricane Katrina made landfall at 6:10 a.m. on August 29, 2005. Barra describes the image of young people fishing in the backwater of a levee as one of the "in-between times [End Page 167] before, after, and around narratives and experiences of climate crisis." The photograph affirms that communities on the frontlines of climate change are not solely defined by risk, vulnerability, and loss "but by their own futures and desires within and beyond the confines of environmental crisis." In an excerpt from her book Before the Streetlights Come On, Heather McTeer Toney states, "Being poor is expensive." She describes how climate disruption most impacts low-income, Black communities located in historically vulnerable regions near industrial facilities and reclaimed land, where the risk of flood and the levels of toxicity are high. The flooding and destruction of the Lower Ninth Ward in New Orleans following Hurricane Katrina was a graphic illustration of this fact, witnessed by thousands of Americans as they watched this horrific event unfold on television and media. The ef-4 rated tornadoes—ef-5 is the highest intensity ranking of a tornado—that tore through the Mississippi Delta and northern Alabama in late March 2023, as we were editing this issue, charted wind speeds near two hundred miles per hour. As contributor Rory Doyle powerfully photographed for the New York Times, many people died and thousands of homes and buildings were destroyed. After touring obliterated Mississippi neighborhoods in Rolling Fork, Silver City, and Winona, Governor Tate Reeves said, "We're going to fight like hell to make sure that we get as many resources to this area as possible." In a region where people of color have been systemically disenfranchised since slavery, Tate's statement is ironic on too many levels to fathom...

title: Of teams and other things
abstract: Figure“The time has come,” the Walrus said, “To talk of many things: Of shoes—and ships—and sealing-wax— Of cabbages—and kings—” —Through the Looking Glass, Lewis Carroll “Team approach” has become a popular medical buzzword, and in our mind's eye we easily envision a perfect interdisciplinary alliance of healthcare experts with diverse expertise. By contrast, traditional medical teams often seem more like restrictive closed shops. In its conventional application, the word team lacks nuance—it simply denotes the involvement of two or more people in some aspect of a patient's care. Such teams are often composed of interchangeable cogs, frequently from a single subspecialty, created for administrative and clinical efficiencies in accomplishing a singular task. That is not always a problem; for many tasks, there really is a best way. A wide variation in skill, experience, philosophy, or training is counterproductive on a venipuncture team. Diversity of thought is detrimental when adherence to evidence-based protocols is essential; everyone on a stroke team should follow the same thrombolytic rules. How, then, should we design an ideal healthcare team? Should membership be multidisciplinary to garner diverse perspectives and fresh insights, or should members be interchangeable clones to guarantee consistency? In reality, medical teams exist for a variety of reasons, and we must know a team's objectives before deciding on its optimal composition. Clear definitions of purpose are essential; vague definitions create confusion and disruption. “When I use a word,” Humpty Dumpty said, in rather a scornful tone, “it means just what I choose it to mean—neither more nor less.” “The question is,” said Alice, “whether you can make words mean so many different things.” —Through the Looking Glass, Lewis Carroll The research study in this month's JAAPA (“Primary care provider type: Are there differences in patients' intermediate diabetes outcomes?” on page 36) takes an important look at one team approach to the outpatient management of diabetes. The composition of the teams (physicians, PAs, NPs) suggests a multidisciplinary approach. In reality, though, clinicians functioned asynchronously as interchangeable providers of equal ability. The result? Intermediate markers of quality of care (A1C, systolic BP, and lipid control) were the same for physician plus PA teams, for physician-only care, and for PA-only care. This is not surprising to anyone familiar with the PA profession, but it is important confirmation of the essential role of the PA profession in optimizing access to superb care for all Americans. A caveat: the intermediate markers measured in the study are important, but they are not the end-all of diabetes care. Patient care is a humanistic endeavor, and the statistical analysis of data sets can never capture the caring part of medicine. Adding a new medication might bring an A1C from 7.5% to 7% and check off a box in the gradebook of “reaching goal”; gaining patient trust while overcoming educational and psychosocial barriers to bring an A1C from 14% to 10% is a far greater accomplishment, but will never show up in the box score of “patients reaching goal.” Preventing a patient's death from hypoglycemia by allowing A1C to drift upward from 6.9% to 7.5% is a therapeutic victory of monumental effect, but it will be listed in the failure column if A1C is the sole marker of quality of diabetes care. Despite the ubiquitous use of statistical data as a surrogate for quality of care, we must remember that clinical excellence often is the result of the intangible components of a therapeutic relationship: “Not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted.”1 As we create newer systems of team-based care and try to measure their value, we should not lose sight of the importance of a primary clinician who is recognized by the patient. Some things in medicine cannot be delegated. Relationship-centered healthcare, the trademark of PA care, is where the magic of medical care takes place. Improving patient health, the ultimate purpose of what we do, usually begins when a trusted provider asks a patient, “What can WE do better?” “We”—the alliance of a patient and a devoted provider—is still the most important medical team ever invented.

title: JUOP June 2025: Personal Time Off With Colleagues—A Unique Approach to Physician Wellness
abstract: PEOPLE, PLACES, AND THINGS In this era of emphasizing wellness, job satisfaction, and avoiding burnout, the summer season of personal time off is a worthy topic of emphasis. Time away with family is certainly important. For this month, I highlight a unique experience of combining time away, personal hobbies, and networking with colleagues. As I have written before (August 2023 and September 2024 issues), Alaska is a favorite destination of mine, and I have traveled with the same charter fishing company since 2015. In the August 2023 issue, I showed pictures from Southeast Alaska with 3 other urology colleagues. This year, that same group of 4 added another 4 urologists—all working as faculty and planners for the North American Robotic Urology Society. Time off with colleagues in an “adventure” mode of travel is a very unique experience. We certainly enjoy talking about our field and how our careers and institutions are progressing. But there is certainly time to talk away from “shop talk” and just enjoy the unique scenery and wildlife. The charter boat only holds 8 guests, so our group was the “whole boat” this time, and each day we mixed and matched the guests with the 2 different guide boats. Each trip has unique opportunities for wildlife, as you never know which animal will get close in for a good shot. The fishing is amazing and the take home catch gives us healthy protein for the year to follow. It is somewhat of a role reversal to go from an attending surgeon managing the operating room team, to a guest on a fishing boat with a guide having the agenda for the day and expertise. Overall, I would highly recommend finding your own opportunity to take an adventure with other urologists and experience networking away from our traditional meeting/society interactions. Figures 1-4 in our People, Places, and Things format highlights the event.Figure 1.: People. Eight urologists on a boat, left to right: Alex Lesani (Las Vegas), Craig Rogers (Detroit), Mike Stifelman (Hackensack), John Davis (Houston), Duke Herrell (Nashville), James Porter (Seattle), Jean Joseph (Rochester), Tom Ahlering (Irvine).Figure 2.: People. Catch of the day—the yellow eye rockfish.Figure 3.: Places. Mist Cove on Baranof Island of Southeast Alaska—home to several salmon fish hatcheries, and a remarkable waterfall coming out of the side of a mountain as a result of draining a glacier lake above. Note our friendly bald eagle on the lookout.Figure 4.: Things—Fabulous Wildlife. A, Not at SeaWorld—an Orca in Chatham Strait of SE Alaska. B, Furry creatures—the Sea Otters float in the bays on their backs and mostly avoid land. C, A juvenile humpback whale showing off its tricks. D, The bald eagle sailing in for a fish.CLINICAL TRIAL RELATED In a prehuman study type of format, Malhotra et al1 performed a bench study on Foley balloon fluid concentrations, specific to a double balloon design intended to improve results in patients with a chronic indwelling catheter. The double balloon design is intended to reduce bladder mucosa injury and obstruction of the eyelet. The results are technical and mostly in line with readers interested in product development. But the editors felt this is such a common issue in urology that only occasionally has technical advances available. Overall, if you care for patients with chronic Foley drainage, have a look at this study and keep an eye out for human studies to follow. RETROSPECTIVE Fidalgo et al2 performed a retrospective study focused on the challenges surrounding complex renal masses, surgical extirpation methods/success rates, and renal function preservation. Of 119 renal cases meeting complex renal mass criteria, 69% were managed with radical nephrectomy and 31% partial. A minimally invasive technique was used in 76%. Renal function preservation correlated with age, extirpation, preoperative function, and ischemia times under 25 minutes. Maintaining glomerular filtration rate over 60 correlated with improved overall survival. Overall, the findings are well known in the literature, but this provides a useful review of a series with useful details on the key variables and outcomes to expect in analyzing one's own results and patient counseling. Prostate pathology and prediction are common and useful areas of study in our field. Sandoval et al3 performed a retrospective in depth study on total length of grade group 4 pattern disease in biopsy samples, as they correlate with pathologic T3 disease on radical prostatectomy specimens. This is a single-institution study but with good sample size. As with most studies of this category, there are the usual array of prognostic factors to consider and statistical comparisons. Figure 1 in the article displays the range of pT3 disease as the total grade group 4 length on biopsy increases—the probably ranges from 38% to 100%. Overall, the data are not only useful for prostatectomy or radiation planning but also in the common clinical challenge of counseling grade group 2 biopsy patients on active surveillance, and the use of percent or total grade pattern 4 to help triage patients to treatment vs surveillance. In the field of renal cell carcinoma, Palmateer et al4 looked at the practical use of the preoperative urinalysis, available on essentially all patients, to correlate with all-cause and cancer-specific mortality for renal cell carcinoma cases treated with nephrectomy. The specific variables studied were blood, protein, nitrites, leukocyte esterase, glucose, and specific gravity—with the first 4 respectively being significant for the survival metrics in a univariate analysis. They looked at additional combinations, and in a multivariate analysis, significant findings included similar. Further work needed would include determining whether any of these features are modified with a treatment plan, and prospective study. Noel et al5 performed a prospective observational cohort study and predictors of urinary diversion choice in patients with bladder cancer. They also did a qualitative analysis, finding 5 main themes of knowledge of diversions, lifestyle implications, education, physician communication, and barriers to care. The predictors studied looked at education, ethnicity, and health literacy. Although both continent and incontinent diversions are standard-of-care choice and have some specific predictors of success and quality of life, this study can help urologists identify patients who might need additional education and counseling, rather than allowing them to settle with physician recommendation only. If you are a qualitative researcher, note the supplemental content showing the interview script. RARE CONDITIONS Hirose et al6 present a rare and instructive case of renal tumors from Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. The patient was already in renal failure and a known left renal mass treated with nephrectomy. Subsequent contralateral tumors were treated with nephrectomy and simultaneous renal transplant. The paper reviews the syndrome, genetics, and associated skin lesions that assisted in the diagnosis.

title: Margaret Atwood, Maddaddam, Bloomsbury, 2013
abstract: Maddaddam is the third and final instalment in Canadian author Margaret Atwood's dystopian trilogy, skilfully blending together the tales of Oryx and Crake (2003) and The Year of the Flood (2007). The two previous books occur over the same timeline, but from different sides of the sociological fence and Maddaddam picks up where the two texts came together. This dark and entirely too likely post-apocalyptic story of survivors could be a joy to read for the scientifically inclined, as each instance of science and technology in the book is possible in our current world. Atwood herself stresses this in her Acknowledgments at the end of the book, stating that 'although Maddaddam is a work of fiction, it does not include any technologies or biobeings that do not already exist, are not under construction or are not possible in theory' (416). Atwood is known to disagree with the genre-label of speculative fiction or dystopia; however, the post-apocalyptic setting and the glimmer of hope for the future carried by her characters evidence her use of the dystopian genre. Though Atwood's depiction and understanding of gene-splicing and current technological capabilities must be praised, her cliched portrayal of computer hacking may roll some eyes - 'Zeb had magic fingers: he could play code the way Mozart played the piano, he could warble the cuneiform, he could waltz through firewalls like a tiger of old leaping through a flaming circus hoop without singeing a whisker' (119). Furthermore, the book claims to take place within the twenty-first century, which is not only a stretch of the imagination, but also dates it uncomfortably close.Atwood tells each book in a dual narrative thread style, creating a curious stylistic blend of oral story-telling and speculative fiction as her characters recount pre-apocalyptic events and struggle to survive in their harsh new world. The survivors are joined by Crakers - fascinating gene-spliced and bio-engineered humanoids designed without human flaws - and it is their naivety that forces readers to revaluate how they see the world as the central character Toby attempts to explain it to them. Questions arise, however, over Toby's nature as an unreliable narrator. We switch from Zeb's version of his past, brutally real, to the watered-down stories Toby then feeds the Crakers and we cannot help but wonder if sheltering them is helping or hindering them in the long-term. Toby, a God's Gardener from The Year of the Flood, takes this storyteller role from Oryx and Crake's Jimmy, or Snowman-the-Jimmy as the Crakers call him, wearing a Red Sox baseball cap and pretending to listen to the words of now-deceased bio-engineer Crake through a plastic watch. The Crakers are almost childlike in their innocence and belief in the all-powerful Crake and uncomfortable parallels can be drawn between them and children. Many of these terms - Crakers, God's Gardeners, Painballers etc. - may cause new readers to struggle and it is obvious that Maddaddam does not work as a standalone book. Too many terms and references are taken for granted as common knowledge within its pages and, as such, the book can only be read after at least one of Oryx and Crake or The Year of the Flood have been read first. Most of the human characters go by the names they took as Crake's bioengineers, which had to be the names of extinct animals, so many new readers and even some readers familiar with the previous books may be confused over the identities of Swift Fox, Ivory Bill, Manatee, Black Rhino, Katuro and Zunzuncito. This confusion turns to amusement with the names of the Crakers, as Crake sought to take human power away from history by naming each Craker after a historical figure:, Abraham Lincoln, Empress Josephine and Blackbeard each grace the pages of Maddaddam.The Crakers aren't the only bio-engineered life forms to make a return appearance in Maddaddam: murderously clever pigs with human brain tissue, originally designed as organ farms, return in force to hound the survivors. …

title: The Way She Looks: A History of Female Gazes in African Portraiture—Photographs from the Walther Collection
abstract: Curated from the holdings of the Walther Collection, The Way She Looks: A History of Female Gazes in African Portraiture was an ambitious photography exhibition that occupied the Main Gallery and the University Gallery of the Ryerson Image Centre in Toronto. In conversation with the bourgeoning interest in African photography and the critical discourse around the fractures in Africa's photographic archives, The Way She Looks attended to gendered subjectivities and centered women as both the subject to the photographer's gaze and the photographer. Photographs spanned from the late nineteenth century to the contemporary period, where the exhibit invited viewers into the bold aesthetics of a geographically diverse collection. Situated as a conversation among creatives, scholars, and art enthusiasts, the show was a retrospective on the diversity and representation of African women behind and in front of the camera, and a cogitation on the futurity of the women's power in African photography.The entryway and lobby bisected the exhibition (Fig. 1), where the Student Gallery held late nineteenth century and early twentieth century black-and-white photographs. The contrast between the two gallery rooms was clear and intentional; in one, subjectivity situated women to the presumed White/outsider photographer's gaze, while in contrast, the Main Gallery's images suggested a conversant and pleasant relationality between African sitter and photographer. In both spaces, several works challenged onlookers to move beyond the commonplace voyeurism associated with colonial portraits and to deeply consider the semiotic power of the gaze throughout the exhibit. The Main Gallery was packed with contemporary photos by African women photographers, mostly from South, West, and East Africa. Colard was steadfast in placing women at the center of the exhibit with the work of female artists such as Yto Barrada, Jodi Bieber, Lebohang Kganye, Zanele Muholi, Grace Ndiritu, and Nontsikelelo “Lolo” Veleko, being accompanied by stunning color portraits by Malian photographers Malick Sibidé and Seydou Keïta. The inclusion of iconic artists like Keïta and Sibidé celebrated the collaborative nature of contemporary portraiture with female sitters. The Way She Looks was about visual intersubjectivities and largely contended with the way the imagined and imaged she is styled and also the ways in which she can conceive and scrutinize real and imaginary worlds from behind and in front of the lens.Zanele Muholi's Miss D'vine II and Samuel Fosso's Autoportrait decoupled gender from sex and masculine-feminine female-male social dictums. With Self-portrait, Angela Davis (2008), Fosso transforms himself into the iconic Black feminist activist, bold colored blouse and Afro intact. Muholi's Mss D'vine II is a gender-nonconforming showcase in a little black dress and red heels with a gender-non-conforming figure, chin held high and regally posed. From the Real Beauty (2008) series, Jodi Bieber's Babalwa (Fig. 2) features a bigger-bodied Black woman with pearls draped as both a choker and stand-in for a blouse to cover her decolletage. The fleshy allure of a white bra and panties is centered in the solitary frame, with the hand-on-hip speaking a near-universal body language that dares and invites viewers to make eye contact. With the placement of Babalwa on an exhibition wall all on its own, the work had a doubling effect; Colard amplified the body positivity of Beiber's portrait, and viewers were pressed to receive brown-skinned beauty and the portraiture's refusal of body shame through a returning female gaze. The absence of clothing indicted any fatphobic responses even as some viewers rushed to pass the piece. In dialectic conversation with JD ‘Okhai Ojeikere's Untitled (Suju Banana Onididi), from the series Hairstyles from 1974 (Fig. 3), the photographs in the modern gallery framed self-possessed imaginaries of beauty, joy, and leisure.In the University Gallery that held images from the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, Colard embraced the somberness that clings to the earlier work's subjunctive qualities. Curatorial notes and labels nudged viewers to peer beyond a banal assent of African women's subjection in colonial portraiture in order to notice the insurrectionary qualities of a sitter's appearance. Riveting images showed women looking back into the camera in oppositional gazes. For the nineteenth century works, object titles such as Bushwoman [sic] and Children (South Africa) and Kaffir [sic] Woman (South Africa) were italicized to indicate how information was directly transcribed from the photographic object. The inclusion of [sic] was a subtle but pointed effort to disrupt the descriptors’ racist hallmarks. In Natives [sic] Hair Dressing, Zanzibar (Tanzania) (Fig. 4), a familiar scene of a young woman styling another's hair was presented in black-and-white. Both women are well dressed, with the white polka-dots of the stylist's shirt playfully framing the hint of a smile on the styled girl's face. The stylist holds an Afro pick, nearly a century before the term became vogue. Colard's selection brought continental historicity to the current natural hair movement for Black women as well as signaling an affirmation to the haptic nature of adornment, care, and wellbeing. The photograph challenges binary thinking about women's agency in nineteenth-century photographs, while also holding space for the possibilities of harm that the sitter endured. In Samuel Baylis Barnard's Bushwoman [sic] and Children (Portrait of !Kweiten ta//ken, 1874–1875) (Fig. 5), the latter theme takes hold. The image immediately beckons the photographic trope of mother and child. The woman is splendidly appointed in earrings, dress, and animal skins. The wispy fur of her cape is the disassociated wings of the naked, cherubesque infant who clings to space just under her bosom. A second child stands at her side, peering to the left. Both children's gazes are preoccupied with the activities off-camera while the woman's gaze divides between left and center. The dual attentiveness places the sitter as an ambivalent subject and spectator, a reposed figure who holds the knowledge of being seen by the camera while also bearing witness to what unfolded outside the frame.In many ways, The Way She Looks was a part of essential conversations about representation and African photographs, the stewardship surrounding their circulation, and the discursive clefts between creative processes and photographic products. Colard's curatorial skills concentrated on the art of looking and seeing through photographic prose, strategic placements, and comprehensive wall labels that engaged the unresolved tensions of ownership and access within African photographs. Each of the selected works interrogated the locus of power to comport unidentified subjects and unnamed photographers and questions who are entitled to wrestle with these themes. Through fashion, beauty, labor, and sexuality, the exhibition staked compelling sensorial and social claims about African women's photographic histories. In all, a crucial display of geographic and chronological breadth regarding gender politics, The Way She Looks, was an unabashed celebration of African women in the visual arts.The Way She Looks: A History of Female Gazes in African Portraiture was organized by the Ryerson Image Centre, Toronto, Canada, in collaboration with The Walther Collection, Neu-Ulm, Germany and New York, USA. The show was supported by media sponsors the Toronto Star, the Walrus, and ByBlacks.com, with additional support from the Ontario Cultural Attractions Fund. With generous funding from the Robert Mapplethorpe Foundation, New York, the show included daily tours as well as four special exhibition tours, including one with the guest curator, Sandrine Colard (Rutgers University), gender studies and feminist scholar Marieme Lo (University of Toronto), Michèle Pearson Clarke, a Trinidadian filmmaker and photographer based in Toronto, as well as local collector, Kenneth Montague. Concurrent with the show, Ryerson Image Centre curator Gaëlle Morel produced a seven-episode podcast, Sightlines, that explores art as activism, the intersections of race and gender in visual art, and the challenges of mainstream representations of Black womanhood.

title: Still Life, and: She Dwells in Violet, and: April 2023
abstract: Still Life, and: She Dwells in Violet, and: April 2023 dg nanouk okpik (bio) Still Life 1 A tempered steel knife piercing my throatbox,Splintered sand silt in my eyes rage itching,A crush of spindled yarn both cruxes can be settledBut too many to untangle knot and frayed ends.At the unraveled present, here now. Here we go;Mukluked feet on my waist a rick-rack ribbon.I trip and fall, fall and trip into slate-blue quicksand,The taste of black licorice in my mouthA digger wasp burrowing into my flesh brown skin.It burns and stings like ice-cold Coca-Cola in my throat. 2 In deep water,Abysmal blackenedThe edge of the roadPotato chip bag,Cigarette butts,Beer bottles,Furrowed as aPrune moth flittersPast me, to gut-edgeOf the cliff's seaside,Marine green waters, [End Page 118] Arsenic land up down,Some part of the surfaceArea: extending upwardMossed rocks and chillWater, warm. EverythingWas damp hot, dimly lit,Crumbling silvers of topsoil.Dim and dank my mind,In an underpinning of a net.I purge and drink, purge.Sea bells on the ridgeway,Or is it the ridgeline? The fur I cut to make a full ruff on my atiguluk parka. In the background, silence.
