title: The Agony and the Ecstasy: International Fieldwork from a Neophyte’s Perspective
abstract: As a postdoctoral scientist at the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH), I am immersed in a long and continuing tradition of expeditionary research. From its earliest days, the American Museum has prided itself on going to the source to get the specimen. The storied expeditions of Barnum Brown (who did his dinosaur hunting in a fur coat) and Roy Chapman Andrews (thought to be the real-life inspiration for Indiana Jones) set a very high standard for a newly minted postdoc. As an evolutionary ecologist, I had of course conducted fieldwork before I arrived at AMNH. My study organisms, moths in the subfamily Heliothinae, are agricultural pests that attack a wide variety of crops. My research into the behavioral differences that distinguish generalist heliothines (those that feed upon plants in numerous families) from specialists (those that feed on a few species in a single plant genus) had led me to the wilds of Georgia, South Carolina, and North Carolina, where I spent weeks sitting in crop fields observing moths, caterpillars, and parasitoids. I had experienced the wearying drudgery of field work; now that I was at AMNH, I was ready for the glamour. The region of maximum diversity for the Heliothinae is the Mata Atlantica of Brazil, which extends along the Atlantic coast of Brazil. The genus I study, Chloridea,1 contains 13 species. Only two of these, Chloridea virescens (Fabricius) and Chloridea subflexa (Guenée), have extended their range into North America, whereas the remainder are found in South and Central America and the Caribbean. I have long dreamed of studying these moths in the region where they originated; sadly, their natal environment is the second most threatened biome on the planet. The Mata Atlantica, which contains a range of tropical forest habitats (dry, moist, and coastal mangrove), once comprised more than 450,000 square miles. Today, less than 38,000 square miles remain, mostly in isolated and degraded patches and in a few nationally or privately protected zones. I was eager to get started on my work as quickly as possible, because there is a real risk of the Mata Atlantica dwindling away to nothing within the next 20 years. My research plan was necessarily fuzzy, because unlike charismatic macrofauna (and even unlike such Lepidopteran beauties as Morpho menelaus (L.), the blue morpho butterfly), chloridean moths are not often observed, reported, or looked for. My starting point was the collection records of my collaborator, Vitor Becker (Fig. 1). Dr. Becker spent many years working for EMBRAPA, the research arm of the Brazilian Ministry of Agriculture, gathering and identifying more than a million specimens of New World moths and butterflies. Upon retirement from EMBRAPA, Dr. Becker and his wife, Clemira, established the Serra Bonita Reserve (SBR) in Bahia, Brazil. Over the past 15 years, the SBR has grown to include almost 20,000 acres of the remaining Mata Atlantica. The SBR land includes undisturbed remnants of the original Mata Atlantica, secondary growth areas that are returning to their natural state after years of use for cacao farming, and recently acquired clear-cut areas that were previously used as pasture land for cattle and as agricultural plots for subsistence farmers. The biodiversity at SBR is amazing, whether one considers primates (four species), birds (400+ species), vascular plants (680 species), amphibians (80 species), or lepidopterans (11,000 estimated species, equivalent to the number found in the U.S. and Canada combined). The SBR also includes a well-equipped research station (Fig. 2), where Dr. Becker’s vast collection of moths and butterflies is housed. Vitor Becker, founder and director of the Serra Bonita Reserve and research station, with Pele, the resident howler monkey. Serra Bonita research station from the air (look for the red tile roof). Photo taken via drone by Bruno Miranda of the SBR. Many species in the group I study have only ever been collected by Dr. Becker, so his collection is the best—often, the sole—guide to where they can be found. However, Dr. Becker is interested in the overall biodiversity of New World Lepidoptera, not just in my small subset of species. Thus, many of his collection records for my species of interest are 15 years old or more, and of course there is no guarantee that species X, found in location Y in 1984, will still be there today. I spent my first month in Brazil at Dr. Becker’s research station, studying his collection and collecting in the surrounding areas. One of my major goals while at the SBR was to catalogue the potential host plants available in the Mata Atlantica. While host plants are not known for all the species I study, the set of known hosts clearly favors a few plant families, primarily Solanaceae, Fabaceae, and Malvaceae. The Solanaceae are of especial interest, because the host plants of many specialist chlorideans are in this family. Thus, I spent many days hiking through the forest collecting and photographing solanaceous plants. Unlike North American Solanaceae (familiar examples of which are tomato, eggplant, potato, and tobacco), South American species range in size from quite small to tree-sized. They are so unlike the plants I am familiar with that it took a few weeks before I was confidently able to identify these “wrong-looking” Solanaceae (Fig. 3). (A) Solanum crinitum, a tree-like Solanaceae from Brazil. Not very tomato-ish! The small green fruit shown here is bigger than a grapefruit when mature. (B) Many Brazilian Solanaceae are blessed with numerous sharp spines…beware! In addition to familiarizing myself with the Solanaceae of the SBR, I spent my days and nights hunting moths. In the daylight, one hopes to find caterpillars feeding. This is the gold standard of determining the host plant range of a species, because when we collect adults, we can only guess at their larval hosts based on the plant species found in the area. And while one can potentially conduct matings between collected moths and then test their larvae on a variety of hosts, finding a male and a female adult at times near enough that their brief lives overlap is chancy. Further, the results of laboratory assays of larval host range are difficult to carry out and can be inaccurate. So, my fingers were permanently crossed as I surveyed potential host plants. Despite finding caterpillar-like damage on a variety of Solanaceae, I found actual chloridean larvae actually feeding in only one instance. Of the species I study, one (C. subflexa) is a specialist on plants in the genus Physalis (Solanaceae). (The best-known Physalis species is philadelphica, commonly known as tomatillo, whose fruits are used in salsa verde.) Physalis species are fast-growing opportunists that love disturbed soil such as old gardens and roadsides, and after many days of driving slowly along bumpy roads (Fig. 4) and poking around abandoned farmsteads, I found several patches of Physalis angulata and pubescens, both known hosts of C. subflexa (Fig. 5). The Land Cruiser. (Dear Mom, thank you for insisting, “Every girl should know how to drive a stick shift!”) The “fruits” of aimlessly driving around: (A) Physalis angulata and (B) Physalis pubescens on the side of a dirt road near Camacan, Bahia. But finding plants (as exciting as that can be even to a non-botanist like me) was not the goal. Determining whether or not Physalis plants have been attacked by C. subflexa is fairly easy because damaged fruits are abscised by the plant, but spotting that is not so easy that you can do it as you drive by. Each plant has to be examined carefully because dropped fruits can work their way into the surrounding understory of grass, and once you do find a damaged plant, you may well be too late to catch a caterpillar. Larvae feed for about two weeks before tunneling into the soil to pupate, and when moth populations are sparse, there might only be caterpillars present every few months. Even when C. subflexa larvae are present, they can be cryptic. The name Physalis comes from the Greek word phusallis, meaning “bladder.” Physalis fruits are surrounded by an inflated calyx (the bladder-y bit), and C. subflexa use this as a refuge from their natural enemies, feeding only when they are fully inside the calyx. Thus, you look for holes in the calyxes and tear them open in the hope that the caterpillar is still inside. The process is a bit hit or miss, but luckily, because I was staying in the area for such a long time, I was able to re-check my plant sites repeatedly. And finally, I found some larvae (Fig. 6)! Chloridea subflexa caterpillar entering the calyx of P. angulata before feeding on the fruit within. While this caterpillar/host plant combination was already well known to me, I was very interested to find that even though many Solanaceae species were present and fruiting, C. subflexa larvae were present only on Physalis angulata. Before visiting Brazil, I had wondered whether the North American characterization of C. subflexa as a narrow host plant specialist might merely reflect a paucity of suitable Solanaceae species in northern climes. After beating the bushes, trees, and grasses in Brazil, I now feel confident that C. subflexa, a widespread and highly successful species, is indeed limited in its host range to no more than three plant species. This leads to some exciting questions about how a species that is so intimately dependent on an ephemeral, annual host that may disappear from a given location from year to year is able to spread so widely and persist so well. As for collecting adults, anyone who studies moths will admit that this is the fun part. Since moths are mostly nocturnal (there are exceptions), the stereotypical lepidopterist with a net, merrily chasing butterflies through a meadow, need not apply. Instead, we take advantage of the still-unexplained fondness of moths for light sources. Armed with a white sheet, a light, and a source of power, we convince the moths to come to us (Fig. 7). The convenience of this system can’t be overstated, but the limitations are serious: at best, you can expect to attract individuals in a 100-meter radius of your light. This attraction radius varies with the power of your light source (fluorescent tube bulbs have a small attraction radius; mercury-vapor bulbs have a wide one); with the species under study (noctuid moths are relatively small and are less likely to visit far-off light sources, whereas sphingid moths, strong flyers with large eyes, will come to light from great distances); with landscape characteristics (lights in high-elevation, unobstructed sites attract more moths than those in dense cover); and with weather and lunar conditions (when the moon is bright, attraction is low, but this can be offset by overcast conditions; surprisingly, moderate rainfall actually increases the abundance of moths visiting a light). In addition, different moth species fly at different times of night, and although some species will land on the lighted sheet and then hang out for hours, others basically do fly-bys, zooming up to the light and then zooming off again without ever landing. Like a moth to a…light bulb? Typical light attraction set-up. Because my goal was to collect a very limited set of species, I was constantly on the watch for one of “my” moths to arrive. I had to be ready to instantly identify and capture the chloridean species I was after, but not to be misled into grabbing anything and everything that looked similar. Of course, different studies have different goals, and a biodiversity survey might take a “one of each” approach, attempting to catch one and only one of every species present (most lepidopterists are also conservationists, and reluctant to collect more specimens than required for their research). Each night at the sheet was full of wonders, and although some visitors were there every night, the overall cast changed radically from day to day, and some species showed up only once in more than a month of lighting. There was no “average” night, but there were some notably busy ones (Fig. 8), and these proved the most challenging: among a horde of flying things, the fear of missing the single visitor that is the object of all one’s efforts can be overwhelming. At times, I felt that even a one-minute absence to answer nature’s call could cost me everything I was striving for. Needless to say, most of the visitors to the sheet were not the species I was after, but because the habits of insects are mysterious, it was impossible to know just which minute of the hundreds I logged at the sheet might be the critical one. To that, add my insecurity about my ability to quickly and correctly identify moths on the wing, and you have the makings of some very stressful nights. “And thick and fast they came at last / And more, and more, and more—“ (From Lewis Carroll’s “The Walrus and the Carpenter,” 1904). Clearly, working alone at the sheet is not ideal. At Serra Bonita, guests at the sheet were mainly non-human, and some were in competition with me for moths (Fig. 9). It was a treat to see owls swooping around and to hear nightjars calling, but the thrill wore off when I realized they were there to scrounge an easy meal from moths flying to or resting on my sheet. (A) Screech owl and (B) nightjar, the fiends who would eat up my moths. Each was about 4 m from the sheet. During my second month in Brazil, I had reinforcements. My collaborator, Cecilia Czepak, at the Universidade Federal de Goiás, is also interested in noctuid moths, but her interest is eminently practical. Dr. Czepak is charged with understanding (and hopefully halting) the recent introduction of Helicoverpa armigera (Hübner), the Old World bollworm, to Brazil. Since its first reported occurrence in 2012, H. armigera has been responsible for millions of dollars of crop losses, particularly in soybean (a major source of biofuel and silage in Brazil). In the United States, the USDA considers it a matter of when, not if, H. armigera will invade. In order for her students to learn a variety of collection techniques, Dr. Czepak offered two of them the chance to go moth hunting with me. I was fortunate that they both agreed, because Esio Dahar Elias and Priscila Veiga Jardim (Fig. 10) were ideal trainees and wonderful travel companions, not to mention far better English-to-Portuguese translators than I. Sara, Esio, and Priscila as a night at the sheet begins. We headed out to the Northeastern region of Goiás to sample a series of sites where Dr. Becker had collected four different species of interest to me. One of these, C. beckeri, has been collected only in this area, and on only two occasions. (One specimen is in the collection at Serra Bonita, and the other is in the Smithsonian. Both were collected by Dr. Becker; hence the patronym.) We used Dr. Becker’s collection data to plot our course, but these collections were made from 12 to 30 years ago. Many former “rural” sites had become suburbs of the growing cities of Planaltina and Brasilia, dirt roads had been paved (or were gone), and landmarks that Dr. Becker had used in the days before GPS reporting were often unidentifiable (Fig. 11). So we mostly relied on the look of the landscape, the vegetation present, and elevation (which had not changed!) in deciding where to explore. This site was savanna cerrado (low woody scrub) in 1985. Now it is a soybean plantation. These rheas, cerrado natives, don’t seem bothered by the change. We started in the north, circumnavigating the Parque Nacional da Chapada dos Veadeiros. title: Reconstructing the Taíno Past: Music, Indigeneity, and Colonialism in Puerto Rico
abstract: This article discusses the significant role that music has played in (re)constructing the Taíno trope in Puerto Rico's collective imaginary. The Taíno were the native people whom Columbus first encountered on his voyages to the New World. Dominant narratives recount that disease, slavery, and war following the Spanish Conquest and colonization of Puerto Rico during the early sixteenth century rapidly extinguished the “docile” Taíno of Borikén (the indigenous name of Puerto Rico) and the neighboring islands of the Caribbean. The Taíno are believed to be descendants of the Arawak peoples who inhabited and still inhabit coastal areas of Venezuela, Suriname, Guyana, and French Guyana.1 Pre-Hispanic contact with neighboring inhabitants of the circum-Caribbean, most notably Carib and Mesoamerican indigenous people, also influenced Taíno language, music, and other aspects of their culture.2The objective of this article is not to discuss the music of the Taíno per se, but rather to provide a historical trajectory of contemporary works that have reconstructed Puerto Rico's indigenous past or used the island's indigenous culture as a source of inspiration. Specific attention will be given to the nineteenth-century nativist opera Guarionex, the indigenist concert music of Héctor Campos Parsi and Ernesto Cordero, the socially engaged nueva canción of Roy Brown, the música urbana of Residente and its close association with the indigenismo movement, and finally the revivalist efforts of the neo-Taíno organization Concilio Taíno Guatu-Ma-Cu A Borikén. Throughout the article I will use the term “indigenist” (also indigenista) in reference to the concert music of Campos Parsi and Cordero. This term is closely related to the late nineteenth- and twentieth-century literary movements known as indianismo and nativismo, which sought to reconstruct and legitimize the official narratives of emerging nation-states in Latin America through the idealized representation of ancient Indian characters, legends, and myths. For its part, indigenismo, though related, refers to the movement that began during the twentieth century in Latin America to advocate for the political, social, and ecological rights of underrepresented indigenous groups. The latter is closely tied to nueva canción and, more recently, música urbana.In the music reconstructions I discuss in this article, Taíno representations are contrasting and ambivalent. In some cases, they evoke nostalgia for a “lost world” whose ecology and lifeways were severely altered, the Taíno as the “good people,” and the myths and spiritual practices that inextricably bound the natives of Borikén to the island's natural habitat. By contrast, other examples celebrate caciques (Taíno chieftains) as warriors of indomitable spirit who never bowed down to colonial oppressors. Whatever the case, the musical reconstructions discussed here speak more about the aesthetic and cultural values of the modern societies that created them than about the Taíno ways of life they intend to represent. The concept of reconstructing highlights the creative processes of appropriation and resignification that this music has impressed on the Taíno past.Reconstructions of Taíno music hinge on two interpretations of Puerto Rico's colonial history. The first narrative, recreated by a creole intelligentsia who sought to legitimize the modern nation-state Estado Libre Asociado (ELA) during the 1950s, views the past as a linear and progressive unfolding of events and establishes that the docile Taíno were conquered and rapidly extinguished by dominant Spanish conquistadores. Remnants of Taíno culture (language, foodways, instruments, spiritual practices) were gradually absorbed through processes of mestizaje3 with European and African populations and survive into the present. The second, more cyclical in nature, reinterprets the events of the Spanish Conquest as something unfinished or unresolved. In this narrative, reconstructed primarily in the popular imaginary, the fierce Taíno are recast as the first heroes to initiate an ongoing battle to reclaim Borikén, a battle still being waged in the present.Both contemporary reconstructions as well as the ancient musical practices of the Taíno remain largely understudied topics in Puerto Rico. This article aims to fill this void by discussing a corpus of music crucial to understanding the development and resilience of Puerto Rico's national identity throughout an uninterrupted colonial history that has spanned over five centuries, first under Spanish rule (1493–1898) and currently under the United States (1898 to the present). Drawing on studies of nativist literature,4 nationalism,5 decoloniality,6 indigeneity,7 environmental history,8 and resistance,9 I compare the political and artistic motivations that reconstruct the
